title: The Bakery's Rising Bread
sum: Over spring break, Mateo helps at Aunt Rosa's bakery before dawn and ends up making and naming a new bread for the Saturday fair.

cast.d: a nine-year-old boy helping at his aunt's bakery over spring break; sleepy at first, full of guesses and names
cast.look: a nine-year-old boy with curly black hair, a white apron that is too big for him and flour on his sleeves

cast.d: Mateo's cousin, eleven, who likes to measure and check everything
cast.look: an eleven-year-old girl with a long dark braid, a green apron and a paper baker's hat

cast.d: Nina's mom and Mateo's aunt, the busy, joking baker who owns Rosa's Bakery on Pine Street
cast.look: a woman in her forties with her hair tied up in a scarf, rolled-up sleeves and a flour-dusted white apron

cast.d: an older neighbor who is the bakery's first customer
cast.look: an older man with gray hair, a flat cap and a tan jacket

cast.d: Mr. Park's little dog, who waits outside on the step
cast.look: a small fluffy brown dog with a red collar

p: Mateo was spending spring break with Aunt Rosa, who lived right above her bakery on Pine Street. On Monday his alarm rang at 4:45, while the sky was still black. He pulled on his socks with his eyes shut and followed his cousin Nina down the back stairs.
The kitchen was bright and hot, and Aunt Rosa had flour on her apron and even more on her nose. “Morning, bakers,” she said. “Wash your hands, and then come and look at this.”

A big steel bowl sat beside the oven, and the towel on top bulged up like a little tent. Mateo lifted one corner and found the dough puffed up over the rim. “At four o'clock, it was only this high,” said Aunt Rosa, holding her hand halfway down the bowl.

Mateo poked the dough with one finger, and it sighed and sank a little. He looked up and asked, “Is it alive?” “The yeast in it is,” said Aunt Rosa. “It's millions of tiny living things that eat the sugar in the flour and breathe out gas.”
She cut a piece off the edge, and the inside was full of little holes, like a sponge. “Bubbles of gas,” she said. “They push the dough up, like air in a balloon.”

“Mom needs a new bread for the street fair on Saturday,” Nina said, tying on her apron. “It needs a name people will remember.” Mateo was suddenly wide awake. “I'm great at names, and I have the best letters in my class,” he said. “I'll make the sign.”

“Deal,” said Aunt Rosa, “but first you're making rolls.” She set a smaller lump of dough on the scale. The numbers jumped around and then stopped at 1,000 grams. “That's all yours. Every roll has to weigh 50 grams, not more and not less.”

Mateo didn't think he needed a scale, because anyone could see how big a roll was. His first ball came out as big as an orange, and the next one was the size of a walnut. Nina weighed them one at a time and read out the numbers, ninety grams and twenty grams.
“That one's a giant, and that one's a baby,” she said. “Customers pay the same for every roll, so they notice.” Mateo's ears went hot as he squished both balls back into the lump and started over.

This time he put every piece on the scale. If it was too heavy, he pulled a little off, and if it was too light, he added a crumb. The flour dust made him sneeze into his elbow, so Nina pointed at the sink without a word.
Then one piece weighed exactly 50 grams on the very first try. Mateo whooped so loud that Aunt Rosa jumped and almost dropped a tray. “Beginner's luck,” she said, but she was laughing.

The rolls rested under a cloth while the oven got hot, and at six o'clock they went in. Twenty minutes later they came out golden brown, and they were all the same size. When Aunt Rosa unlocked the door at 6:30, the first customer was an old neighbor named Mr. Park.

He bought two rolls and bit into one at the counter, while his little dog Biscuit watched through the glass. “Good,” he said with his mouth full. “Who made these?” Mateo held up one floury hand, and out on the step, Biscuit wagged his whole back end.

art.s: In a bright bakery kitchen before dawn, a sleepy nine-year-old boy in a too-big apron lifts a towel off a huge bowl of puffy dough while his older cousin and his aunt watch.

q.q: Draw the dough at four o'clock, and then again when Mateo lifted the towel. Show what the tiny bubbles did.
look: a small lump of dough, then a much bigger one
little bubbles inside the bigger dough
the towel pushed up like a tent
q.e: The yeast made bubbles, and the bubbles pushed the dough up. You showed it rising!

q.q: What is this story mostly about?
c: Mateo walks down the stairs in the dark
Mateo learns to make rolls that are all the same size
Mr. Park buys two rolls for breakfast
Aunt Rosa shows Mateo a bowl of dough
q.e: All of these happen, but most of the story is about Mateo getting his rolls to 50 grams each.

q.q: Mateo's dough weighed 1,000 grams. Each roll had to be 50 grams. How many rolls could he make?
q.e: 1,000 ÷ 50 = 20. That's twenty rolls, all the same size.

eps.t: The Warm Cup and the Cold Cup
p: On Tuesday the back room was freezing, because somebody had left the window open all night. Nobody would say who. In the corner, the big tub of dough sat flat and quiet. Aunt Rosa lifted the lid and frowned. “An hour in here, and it's hardly moved,” she said.

Mateo knew how that felt, because he had hardly moved either. He stood by the oven with his hands out, as if it were a campfire. “Maybe it's too cold,” he said. “I don't want to do anything when I'm cold.”

“Yeast is just like you,” said Aunt Rosa. “When it's cold, it goes slow, and when it's warm, it gets busy and makes lots of bubbles.” She carried the tub to the shelf above the oven. Nina crossed her arms and said, “Dough is dough. The room can't matter that much.”

Mateo had an idea. He found two tall, clear plastic cups, the kind for iced drinks. Nina weighed out two lumps of dough, 100 grams each, and pressed one into each cup. Both lumps stood 3 cm tall. Only one thing would be different, and that was where the cups sat.

The warm cup went on the shelf above the oven. The cold cup went on the windowsill, right by the open window. On the back of an order pad, Mateo drew a table with three columns: time, warm cup and cold cup. In the first row he wrote 5:15, 3 cm and 3 cm.

Mateo asked, “So which one will win?” “Neither,” said Nina. “They'll be about the same, or maybe the cold one will be a little slower.” Mateo rubbed his cold ears. “The warm one will win by a lot,” he said, “because yeast is like me.”

While they waited, Mateo tried out names for the fair bread, starting with Bubble Bread. “That sounds like soap,” said Nina. He tried Puff Loaf next, but Nina said it sounded like a pillow. Aunt Rosa slid a tray of rolls into the oven and said, “Keep thinking.”

At 5:45 they checked on the cups. The warm cup had grown to 4 cm. Through the clear plastic, Mateo could see tiny bubbles pressed against the side, like the bubbles in soda. The cold cup was still 3 cm tall, with only a few small bubbles near the bottom.

At 6:15, when they checked again, the sky above the rooftops was turning pink. “The sun's rising,” said Nina. “Everything rises early around here,” said Aunt Rosa, “the sun, the bread and Nina.” She grinned at Mateo. “But not you.”

The warm cup had puffed all the way up to 6 cm, twice as tall as when they started. The cold cup had only crept up to 4 cm. Mateo wrote both numbers in the last row of his table and drew a big star next to the 6.

Nina stared at the two cups for a long time, tapping first the warm one and then the cold one. “Okay,” she said at last. “Maybe dough isn't just dough.” Mateo wrote that on the order pad too, word for word, and underlined it twice.
Then Nina shut the back window with a bang. Mateo carried the cold cup over to the warm shelf and set it next to the tall one. “Your turn,” he told it.

art.s: Two children in aprons compare two clear plastic cups of dough, one tall and bubbly on a warm shelf above an oven and one short on a cold windowsill, while a pink dawn sky shows through the window.

q.q: Draw a bar graph of the two cups at 6:15. Make one bar for the warm cup and one bar for the cold cup.
look: the warm bar up to 6 cm and the cold bar up to 4 cm
the warm bar taller than the cold bar
q.e: The graph shows it at a glance: the warm cup grew more.

q.q: Why did the dough in the warm cup rise higher than the dough in the cold cup?
q.a: Yeast works faster when it is warm, so it made more bubbles.
q.e: Just like Aunt Rosa said, warm yeast gets busy. More bubbles make more rise.

q.q: Nina said, “The sun's rising.” What does rising mean there?
c: getting puffy with bubbles
getting out of bed
coming up in the sky
growing taller like a plant
q.e: Rise has many meanings. Bread rises, people rise from bed, and the sun rises into the sky.

p: On Wednesday, Aunt Rosa took an old recipe card out of a tin box. Its corners were soft, and a brown honey spot sat right in the middle. “Grandma Lupe's Honey Oat Bread,” Nina read. “Makes 4 loaves.” When Mateo sniffed the card, it still smelled a little like honey.

“Let's try it for the fair,” said Aunt Rosa, “but only 2 loaves today, in case it's bad.” She pushed a big tray toward the stove. “Make half of everything,” she said. “You two can do it while I boil 60 bagels.”

Nina read the card out loud, and Mateo wrote the halves on a sticky note. Six cups of flour became 3, and two cups of warm water became 1. Four big spoons of honey became 2, and the yeast and the salt each went from 2 teaspoons to 1. The card said 1 cup of oats, so they needed ½ cup.

The ½-cup scoop was missing, and only the little ¼-cup scoop was left in the drawer. Mateo did the math in his head and scooped the oats into the bowl. Nina added the honey, which slid off the spoon in a slow, golden rope.

Next, Mateo picked up the measuring jug. He looked at the recipe card instead of the sticky note, and he poured in two cups of warm water. Then he stirred with a big wooden spoon. Slurp, slosh, slurp, slosh.

The dough was not turning into a ball. It was a thick, lumpy puddle that grabbed Mateo's fingers when he reached in. As he pulled his hand out, long sticky strings came with it, like melted cheese on a pizza. He held up his hand and asked, “Why is it soup?”

Nina looked from the sticky note to the empty jug and asked, “How much water did you put in?” “Two cups,” said Mateo. “The note says 1,” said Nina, and Mateo groaned. Aunt Rosa came over, drying her hands on her apron, and poked the puddle with one finger.

“Flour drinks up water, like a sponge,” said Aunt Rosa. “But 3 cups of flour can only drink so much, and you gave it too much.” Mateo wiped his gloopy fingers on a towel and asked, “So do we throw it away?” “Never,” she said. “We make the whole recipe instead.”

So they added the other half of everything. Three more cups of flour went in a little at a time, and then more oats, honey, yeast and salt. Bit by bit, the puddle got thicker. At last it was a real ball of dough, smooth and a little bouncy. It let go of Mateo's hands.

“Half and half make a whole,” said Nina. “Now we'll have 4 loaves.” Mateo licked some honey off his thumb and said, “More bread isn't a problem.” The loaves went into the oven with oats sprinkled on top.

While they baked, Mateo made a sign for the test bread and wrote HONEY OAT BREAD in his best letters. Nina read it and wrinkled her nose. “Boring,” she said. “Why would anyone buy it?” Mateo thought about the bread for a minute, and then he added three words under the name: SOFT, SWEET, CRUNCHY.

By eight o'clock, the four loaves sat on the rack, brown and shiny with toasted oats on top. Aunt Rosa cut the smallest one and tasted a slice without saying a word. Then she took a second slice. “It tastes like my mother's kitchen,” she said, and Nina grinned at Mateo. “That means yes.”

art.s: At a floury counter, a boy holds up his hand covered in sticky strings of dough over a bowl while his cousin points at a yellow sticky note and an old recipe card.

q.q: Mateo needed ½ cup of oats, but he only had a ¼-cup scoop. How many scoops did he need?
q.e: Two quarters make a half: ¼ + ¼ = 2/4, and 2/4 is the same as ½.

q.q: Draw Mateo's sign for the honey oat bread. Use his describing words or your own.
q.e: Good describing words let people taste the bread before they buy it.

q.q: Why did Mateo's dough turn into a sticky puddle?
c: It had too much water for the flour to soak up.
The honey was too thick to mix in.
The oats soaked up all the flour.
The yeast made too many bubbles.
q.e: Flour drinks water like a sponge. Two cups of water was too much for 3 cups of flour.

p: On Friday, the day before the fair, they made Grandma Lupe's whole recipe in the big bread pans. Aunt Rosa shaped the loaves and set them in their pans at 5:10. “Now they rise for 45 minutes,” she said. “Mateo, you're in charge of the timer.”

Mateo set the timer on the shelf by the oven and pressed start. He watched the numbers count down like a guard until Nina tugged his sleeve. “It counts by itself,” she said. “Come and help with the truck.”

A delivery truck had backed up to the side door, and the driver was stacking twelve flour sacks. Each sack weighed 25 kilograms, almost as much as Mateo. It took both cousins to drag one sack to the storeroom. Back in the kitchen, the big mixer roared as it stirred dough for tomorrow.

In the storeroom, Mateo counted sacks while Nina wrote them down. The mixer was so loud that they had to shout every number twice. Somewhere under all that noise, a small timer beeped and beeped, but nobody heard it.

At 6:25, Mateo walked back into the kitchen and froze. The loaves had puffed up high over the tops of their pans, like giant mushrooms. He grabbed the timer, which said 0:00 and had stopped beeping a long time ago.

Aunt Rosa looked at the pans and sighed. “Too long,” she said, “but let's bake them and see.” Mateo watched the tops through the little oven window. At first they looked fine, but then the middles began to sag, like a tent with its pole pulled out.

The loaves came out flat and wrinkly, with a dent down the middle of each one. Mateo's stomach dropped, and he said, “The fair is tomorrow, and I wrecked it.” Aunt Rosa cut one open. The holes inside were big and torn instead of small and round.

“The yeast kept going,” she said. “The bubbles got bigger and bigger until they stretched too thin and popped, like a balloon blown up too far.” She pressed the soft middle with her thumb. “After that, nothing was left to hold the loaf up.”

Mateo stared at the flat loaves, and his eyes felt hot. Aunt Rosa bumped him with her elbow. “My first loaf was as flat as a pancake,” she said. “Grandma Lupe used it as a doorstop for a week.” Nina snorted, and even Mateo laughed a little.

They started a new batch right away. When the new loaves went into their pans, Mateo pressed start and dropped the timer into his apron pocket. “Nobody leaves the kitchen,” he said, and Nina saluted him with a wooden spoon.

Forty-five minutes later, his pocket went bzzt, bzzt against his leg. Mateo jumped so high that he nearly hit the shelf. The loaves were round and puffy, just a little above the pans. Into the oven they went, and this time the tops stayed up, tall and brown.

The flat loaves didn't go to waste either. Aunt Rosa sliced them thin, brushed them with butter and toasted them until they crunched. Nina held one up and asked, “Should we call it Pancake Bread?” Mateo took a big, loud bite and said, “Not on my sign.”

art.s: In a bakery kitchen, a boy in an apron stares in dismay at a row of flat, wrinkly loaves on a cooling rack while his aunt holds one cut open and his cousin peeks over his shoulder.

q.q: Draw Mateo when he saw the flat loaves. Add a speech bubble with what Aunt Rosa said to cheer him up.
look: a speech bubble with Aunt Rosa's words
q.e: A kind joke can help on a bad morning. You showed how Mateo felt!

q.q: Why did the first loaves sink in the oven?
q.a: They rose too long, so the bubbles stretched too thin and popped.
q.e: Too much rising stretches the bubbles until they pop. Then nothing holds the loaf up.

q.q: The loaves started rising at 5:10. Mateo came back at 6:25. How long did they rise?
c: 45 minutes
65 minutes
85 minutes
75 minutes
q.e: From 5:10 to 6:10 is 60 minutes, and 15 more makes 75. That's 30 minutes too long.

p: On Saturday, Mateo woke up before his alarm. It was 4:30 and still dark, but he wasn't sleepy at all. He was downstairs before Nina even had her shoes on. Aunt Rosa looked up from the mixer. “Who are you,” she said, “and what did you do with Mateo?”

Aunt Rosa had started the fair dough at three o'clock, and all morning it rose on the warm shelf. By six, 48 honey oat loaves sat cooling on the racks, their tops shining golden brown from the honey. The cousins packed them into 4 baskets, with the same number in each.

The fair was in the little park at the end of Pine Street. They carried the baskets and a folding table down the sidewalk in the gray light. At the east end of the street, the sky over the river was turning orange. At the west end, the full moon hung low over the church roof, round and pale like a paper plate.

Mr. Park and Biscuit were already there. He pointed down the street one way and then the other. “The sun's coming up and the moon's going down, both at once,” he said. “That's because we live on a big spinning ball. Right now it's turning us toward the sun and away from the moon.”
Just then, the sun peeked over the river. Its light fell across the baskets, and every loaf lit up gold. Mateo looked at the sun, then at the bread, and then he grabbed the chalk.

The little chalkboard for the stall had been blank all week. Now Mateo wrote SUNRISE LOAF across it in his biggest, best letters. Under that he wrote “Honey, oats and a very early morning” and the price, $6. In the corner he drew a small sun with long rays.

Nina read the board and asked, “Why Sunrise?” “Because it rises before the sun does, and it's gold like the sun,” said Mateo. Nina read the board a second time. “Okay,” she said, “that one's not boring.”

At seven o'clock the fair opened, and Mr. Park bought the very first loaf. “It's for me and a little bit for Biscuit,” he said. Biscuit's tail thumped against the table leg. After that, more and more people came, so Mateo took the money and Nina counted out the change.

Aunt Rosa cut one loaf into 8 slices for tasting. She set them on a plate next to a sign that said FREE TASTE. In ten minutes, 5 slices were gone. A man in running shoes ate one, jogged away and came back to buy two loaves.

By 9:15 the baskets were empty. A woman in a green hat looked at the bare table and asked, “No more Sunrise Loaf?” “Come to the bakery on Monday,” said Aunt Rosa. Then she turned to Mateo and said, “I guess it's on the menu now.”

Back at the bakery, Aunt Rosa set up the stepladder under the big menu board. It said Plain Rolls, Rye and Cinnamon Twist in her neat white letters. She handed Mateo the chalk and said, “Bottom line, big letters.”

Mateo climbed up and wrote SUNRISE LOAF. Next to it he drew a small sun, just like the one at the fair. Chalk dust drifted down onto the counter. When he climbed down, Nina handed him a warm roll. He didn't even weigh it.

art.s: At sunrise in a small park at the end of a city street, a boy writes SUNRISE LOAF on a chalkboard beside baskets of golden loaves, with the sun rising over a river at one end of the street and a pale full moon setting over a church at the other.

q.q: Why did Mateo name the bread the Sunrise Loaf? Give one reason.
q.a: It rises before the sun does, and it is gold like the sun.
q.e: Mateo had two good reasons: the bread rises early, and it is gold like the sun.

q.q: Aunt Rosa cut one loaf into 8 slices. People ate 5 of them. What fraction of the loaf was left?
q.e: 8 slices take away 5 leaves 3. Three slices out of eight is 3/8.

q.q: Draw Pine Street at sunrise on Saturday. Show where the sun was and where the moon was.
look: the sun coming up on one side, over the river
the round moon low on the other side, over the church
the golden loaves at the stall
q.e: The sun and the full moon were on opposite sides of the sky. You looked like a real sky watcher!

fin.q: This week Mateo learned two ways to help dough rise just right. What are they?
fin.a: Keep the dough warm, and don't let it rise too long.
fin.e: The cup test showed that warm yeast works faster. Friday's flat loaves showed what happens when dough rises too long.

fin.q: What is the whole story mostly about?
c: Mateo learns to make rolls that weigh 50 grams.
Nina and Mateo test a warm cup and a cold cup.
Mateo helps make a new bread for the fair and gives it a name.
Mr. Park walks Biscuit to the bakery every morning.
fin.e: Each morning was one step toward the fair. The whole story is about making and naming the Sunrise Loaf.
